title: Longest Common Subsequence
statement: Given two strings, return the length of their longest common subsequence. A subsequence is what is left after deleting zero or more characters without reordering the rest, so the characters must appear in the same order in both strings but need not be adjacent. Return 0 if there is none.
realWorld: This is what diff computes: the lines a patch leaves untouched are the longest common subsequence of the two files, and everything else is an insertion or a deletion. The same table drives three-way merges, rsync-style delta encoding, and DNA sequence alignment.

examples.explanation: 'ace' appears in order inside 'abcde' — the b and d are deleted. Adjacency is not required.
'GTAB' is a subsequence of both. The longest common *substring* (contiguous) is only one character long, which is why this example separates the two ideas.
No character is shared, so the answer is the empty subsequence.

constraints: Both strings consist of lower-case or upper-case English characters
Characters may repeat inside a string

bruteForce.idea: Recurse on the two ends. If the last characters match, that pair belongs to the answer and both strings shrink by one. If they differ, one of the two last characters cannot be in the answer — try dropping each and take the better result.
code: public static int longestCommonSubsequence(String a, String b) {
private static int lcs(String a, String b, int i, int j) {
if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) return 1 + lcs(a, b, i - 1, j - 1);
return Math.max(lcs(a, b, i - 1, j), lcs(a, b, i, j - 1));
bruteForce.whySlow: On a mismatch the recursion forks into (i-1, j) and (i, j-1), and those two branches overlap almost completely — both of them reach (i-1, j-1), which then re-explodes below. With two strings of length 20 the tree has on the order of 2^40 leaves while there are only 21 x 21 = 441 distinct (i, j) pairs in the entire problem, so the average pair is recomputed billions of times. The pair (10, 10) alone is reached from every path that has consumed ten characters of each string, which is C(20,10) = 184,756 different ways.

patternIdentification: Two sequences compared, with an answer that depends on a position in each → the state is two-dimensional, indexed by a prefix of one and a prefix of the other. Name it first: dp[i][j] = the length of the LCS of the first i characters of a and the first j characters of b. Then ask the only useful question — what can happen at the last pair of characters? Either they are equal, in which case pairing them is never a mistake (any answer that skips a match can be rewritten to include it without getting shorter), so dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; or they differ, in which case at least one of them is not used, so try discarding each and keep the better: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Base cases are the empty prefixes: dp[0][j] = dp[i][0] = 0. This is the same grid as edit distance — identical shape, identical neighbours, different cost on each move — and recognising that one table serves both is what makes the next two-sequence problem easy.

optimized.idea: Fill the (m+1) x (n+1) grid row by row. The extra row and column hold the empty-prefix base cases, which is why the strings are indexed with i-1 and j-1. Each cell reads only its top, left and top-left neighbours, so the table can be collapsed to two rows — or one row plus a saved diagonal value — for O(min(m, n)) space when memory matters.

complexity.space: O(m * n), reducible to O(min(m, n))

commonMistakes: Solving longest common *substring* by mistake: setting dp[i][j] = 0 on a mismatch instead of taking the max. Contiguity is then required, and 'AGGTAB' against 'GXTXAYB' returns 1 instead of 4 — the sample with adjacent matches still passes, so the bug hides well.

Indexing the strings with i and j instead of i-1 and j-1 while dp has m+1 rows. The last row asks for charAt(m) and throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException; if you also shrink the loop bounds to hide that, the final character is never compared and every answer that ends in a match is short by one.

Collapsing to a single row without saving the diagonal first. By the time you read dp[j-1] it already holds the current row's value rather than the previous row's, so the match branch adds to the wrong cell and the result comes out too large on strings with repeated characters — keep the old dp[j-1] in a temporary before overwriting it.
